methodological_rigor.justification: The retrospective single-institution cohort design is appropriate for the question, but the analysis fails to address substantial baseline imbalances. OBCS patients were younger, had fewer comorbidities, larger/higher-stage tumors, more multifocal disease, and higher nodal burden, yet no propensity score matching, multivariable regression, or adjusted Cox models were performed — only unadjusted t-tests, chi-square, and log-rank tests. Median follow-up differed significantly between groups (5.54 vs 4.64 years, p<0.0001) and between OBCS Level I vs II subgroups, which materially affects recurrence/DFS comparisons that were nonetheless interpreted as equivalence. No power/sample-size calculation is reported, no multiplicity correction is applied across many simultaneous comparisons, missing data handling is described only as 'appropriately accounted for' without specifics, and the equivalence claim is drawn from non-significant p-values rather than a formal equivalence/non-inferiority framework with pre-specified margins.

clinical_relevance_loe.justification: This is an individual retrospective cohort study of 1290 breast cancer patients (Oxford LoE 2b) with ~5-year median follow-up. The question — whether OBCS compromises oncologic safety or delays adjuvant therapy — is clinically meaningful for breast surgical decision-making, and endpoints include patient-relevant outcomes (locoregional recurrence, DFS, time to adjuvant therapy, complications). However, the findings largely confirm a well-established literature already supporting OBCS safety and are unlikely to change practice or guidelines; relevance is moderate rather than practice-changing, especially given the unadjusted analysis limits the strength of the safety claim.

reporting_quality.justification: STROBE is the applicable standard; the manuscript explicitly states adherence and provides a patient flow diagram (Figure 1), eligibility criteria, outcome definitions, and REB approval. Key STROBE items are only partially addressed: no description of handling missing data beyond a one-line statement, no quantification of missingness per variable, no sensitivity analyses, no reporting of effect sizes with 95% CIs for primary comparisons, and limited discussion of bias/confounding strategies despite marked baseline differences. There is no statement of data or code availability, no mention of a public repository, and no analytic code shared, warranting a low reproducibility score.

novelty_literature.justification: The study is incremental: the OBCS-vs-lumpectomy comparison has been addressed in numerous prior single- and multi-institution series, systematic reviews, and meta-analyses, many of which are cited (refs 2, 3, 5, 14, 28, 30, 32, 34, 44, 48, 49, 52). The authors' main novelty claim — 'largest-scale Canadian analysis' — is a geographic/scale increment rather than a conceptual or methodological advance. Findings (equivalent oncologic outcomes, slightly more minor complications, modest radiotherapy delay) replicate prior conclusions without introducing new mechanisms, techniques, or populations, and the manuscript does not offer a novel analytic framework or biomarker component.

writing_presentation.justification: The manuscript is generally readable with a conventional IMRaD structure, clearly defined outcomes, and an abstract that reflects the main findings quantitatively. There is noticeable redundancy (e.g., chemotherapy sequencing paragraph in 3.3 largely restates the preceding text; the symmetry-procedure discussion is repeated in paragraph form in the Discussion), a typographical error ('p > 0.0.5'), and some inconsistencies between abstract and body (e.g., mean age 56 vs. 56.5; percentages such as 40.0% vs 40.1%). Table/figure captions are referenced but not visible; results text occasionally mixes SDs and ranges without clarity, and the Discussion is dense and could be tightened to avoid rehashing results.

key_strengths: Large single-institution cohort (n=1290) with ~5-year median follow-up and no loss to follow-up
Clinically meaningful outcome set spanning complications, time to adjuvant therapy, recurrence, and DFS
STROBE-aligned reporting with a patient flow diagram, pre-defined major/minor complication criteria, and dual-reviewer data abstraction with a third adjudicator
Stratification of OBCS by Level I vs Level II provides useful granularity on technique-related morbidity
key_concerns: No multivariable or propensity-score adjustment despite major baseline imbalances in age, comorbidities, tumor size, stage, focality, and nodal status — equivalence claims for oncologic outcomes are unadjusted
Follow-up duration differs significantly between groups (5.54 vs 4.64 years, p<0.0001) and across OBCS levels, potentially biasing recurrence/DFS comparisons interpreted as 'no difference'
No power/sample-size calculation; equivalence is inferred from non-significant p-values rather than a formal non-inferiority framework with pre-specified margins
No multiplicity correction across numerous simultaneous comparisons; effect sizes with 95% CIs are not reported for primary endpoints
Novelty is limited — findings largely replicate an extensive prior literature already cited in the discussion
No data or code availability statement; missing-data handling is only vaguely described
chief_reviewer.rationale: This is a competent but highly incremental single-center retrospective cohort whose unadjusted analyses cannot credibly support the equivalence claims given the substantial baseline and follow-up imbalances. The scale and clinical topic suit a Tier 4 oncology/surgery journal, but major revisions — including propensity-matched or multivariable adjusted analyses, formal non-inferiority framing, and effect sizes with 95% CIs — are needed before acceptance.
